title: Superlattice Engineering Stabilizes Bulk‐to‐Surface Microenvironment in Single‐Crystalline Ultrahigh‐Ni Cathodes
content:
This work demonstrates the construction of an ordered Li/Ni anti‐site superlattice in single‐crystalline ultrahigh‐Ni LiNi0.93Co0.02Mn0.03Al0.02O2 cathodes via Mo‐induced microenvironment regulation, delivering a high reversible capacity and excellent cycling stability. This is the first time to achieve a bulk‐local‐pinned and surface‐even‐distributed superlattice structure in micro‐sized single‐crystalline materials, significantly lowering the Li‐ion diffusion barrier, suppressing oxygen loss, and restraining c‐axis contraction.








ABSTRACT
Single‐crystalline ultrahigh‐Ni cathodes hold great promise for high‐energy Li‐ion batteries, but their practical adoption is hindered by sluggish delithiation kinetics and severe structural degradation. Although superlattice engineering has been established as an effective strategy to stabilize lattice oxygen and enhance Li‐ion diffusion in polycrystalline counterparts, realizing ordered Li/Ni anti‐site superlattices in micro‐sized single‐crystalline materials remains challenging, as their formation is largely restricted to the near‐surface region. Herein, we report for the first time the construction of a bulk‐locally‐pinned and surface‐even‐distributed ordered Li/Ni anti‐site superlattice structure in single‐crystalline ultrahigh‐Ni LiNi0.93Co0.02Mn0.03Al0.02O2 cathodes via Mo‐induced local microenvironment regulation during high‐temperature lithiation. The resulting cathodes exhibit a 32% reduction in Li‐ion diffusion energy barrier, a 23% decrease in lattice oxygen loss, and a 26% suppression of c‐axis lattice contraction at 90% state of charge. Consequently, these improvements effectively alleviate stress concentration and substantially accelerate delithiation kinetics. The optimized cathode delivers an ultrahigh reversible capacity of 230 mAh g−1 at 0.1C and achieves a cycle life exceeding 4500 cycles in Ah‑level pouch‐type full cells.

title: Microfluidic‐Enabled Elastic Photothermal Helical Gel Microfibers for High‐Efficiency Solar Evaporation With Spatially Regulated Light‐Thermal‐Water Management
content:
An elastic photothermal helical gel microfiber evaporator with spatially coordinated light‐thermal‐water management, achieves efficient photothermal conversion, optimized solar heat localization, water supply and salt rejection for efficient interfacial water evaporation. Leveraging its flexibility, the evaporator affords bending requirements in a solar‐tracking system, demonstrating a highly adaptive and scalable solution for clean water production.








ABSTRACT
Fibrous films and fabrics have been extensively employed for solar photothermal interfacial evaporation due to their high specific surface area, flexibility and scalability. However, the inherent planar geometry of fibrous films/fabrics restricts the evaporation area, and vapor/mass diffusion, limiting the evaporation efficiency and inducing salt accumulation. Herein, we propose a strategy of shifting the planar fabrics to photothermal helical microfiber evaporators via microfluidic technology, featuring intrinsic three‐dimensional structure, prominent elasticity and flexibility. The distinctive central cavity in helical gel microfibers enables spatial regulation of light, thermal and water transport, not only expanding evaporation area but also efficiently localizing thermal energy and capturing additional energy. By tuning the helical pitch, the water transport, vapor diffusion and light capture capabilities are synergistically optimized, achieving an evaporation rate of 3.65 kg m−2 h−1 under 1 sun irradiation with superior salt resistance. Moreover, the excellent flexibility of the helical microfiber fabric imparts exceptional structural adjustability, allowing to perform solar‐tracking evaporation. Outdoor tests using such solar‐tracking system with enlarged evaporation area deliver a stable evaporation rate of 8.57 kg m−2 h−1 under solar intensity of ∼950 W m−2, which demonstrates a viable design concept for high‐performance fabric‐based evaporators in sustainable solar interfacial evaporation.

title: AR/PARP Dual‐Targeting Bioactive Photosensitizer for Photo‐Immunotherapy of Prostate Cancer
content:
Prostate cancer poses a severe threat to men's health worldwide, and conventional therapeutic modalities are associated with various limitations. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) offers distinctive advantages such as minimal invasiveness, mild side effects, and repeatable treatment. However, the therapeutic efficacy of PDT is limited by two critical factors: the single functional property of traditional photosensitizers and the pathological tumor microenvironment. Accordingly, molecular targeting photosensitizers have been developed to address these drawbacks. Notably, long‐term administration of single‐target agents entails a high risk of drug resistance. Accordingly, based on two key targets closely implicated in the DNA repair pathways of prostate cancer cells, the androgen receptor (AR), and poly(ADP‐ribose) polymerase (PARP), we proposed an AR/PARP dual‐targeting photosensitizer strategy and synthesized a quinoxalinone‐based photosensitizer QTEO, which can simultaneously target AR and PARP and exert a synergistic effect with photodynamic activity to induce DNA damage in cancer cells. The resulting damaged DNA fragments can further activate the innate immune pathways of the organism through a coordinated cascade of reactions. This promising strategy concurrently overcomes the limited functionality of conventional photosensitizers, the potential drug resistance induced by single‐target agents, and the complex pharmacokinetic issues associated with multidrug combination therapy, ultimately enabling molecular‐targeting photo‐immunotherapy for prostate cancer.

title: Atomic‐Scale CuTe/PdTe Intermetallic Heterointerface Enhances Electrochemical Glycerol Oxidation
content:
Using a strategy guided by crystal seed epitaxial nucleation, we have precisely synthesized an atomic‐scale ternary Pd‐Cu‐Te intermetallic catalyst with precise bonding at the interface. The synthesized catalyst promotes the hydroxyl adsorption and dehydrogenation of the glycerol intermediate through atomic bonding at the interface, thereby facilitating C–C bond cleavage.








ABSTRACT
Intermetallic materials have shown great potential for electrocatalytic molecular valorization, benefiting from their abundant intrinsic active sites. However, synthesizing intermetallic electrocatalysts with unique atomic‐scale interfacial structures remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report the synthesis of a previously unknown ternary intermetallic nanowire with exquisite atomic‐scale interfaces, achieved through optimal crystal facets mediated selective phase alloying. At the phase interface, the PdTe <100> {001} plane is parallel to the CuTe <0−11> {100} plane, achieving quasi‐epitaxial bonding. This orientation relationship demonstrates high structural coherence at the PdTe‐CuTe interface and minimizes interfacial strain. The novel structure is rich in interfacial active sites, facilitating the overcoming of the slow catalytic oxidation kinetics. The glycerol oxidation selectivity of the as‐prepared interface‐enriched catalysts is highly enhanced with an ultra‐high Faradaic efficiency of 96.5% toward formate at 1.425 V. In situ spectra and theoretical calculations demonstrate that the enriched Pd‐Cu‐Te ternary interfaces can optimize the adsorption configuration of glycerol, accelerating the subsequent O‐H cleavage of *COOHCOCH2OH and C–C cleavage. This approach paves the way to rationally designed intermetallic catalysts with modified interfaces for biomass electrooxidation.

title: In Situ Polymerized Scaffolds Imposing Large Compressive Stress for High‐Performance Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
In situ additive polymerization converts detrimental tensile stress into substantial compressive strain in perovskite films via thermo‐mechanical anchoring. This stress reversal exhibits a linear correlation with device efficiency, delivering a champion PCE of 26.53% for FAMA perovskite with exceptional stability. Validated across diverse additives and compositions, this universal strategy establishes strain engineering as a foundational design principle for high‐performance PCEs.









ABSTRACT
Metal halide perovskite solar cells have achieved remarkable efficiencies but remain constrained by operational instability, intrinsically linked to mechanical strain within the polycrystalline films. Existing strategies primarily mitigate harmful tensile stress, yet lack the capacity to introduce substantial, beneficial compressive strain. Here, we develop a universal “thermo‐mechanical anchoring” strategy that imposes large compressive stress via in situ polymerization of a designed monomer in the perovskite matrix. This method enables broad‐range control of film stress, converting substantial tensile stress into pronounced compressive strain (up to 36.05 MPa), experimentally validating a positive correlation between compressive stress and device performance. The polymer network, with a high thermal expansion coefficient and strengthened adhesion, contracts more than the perovskite during cooling, mechanically pulling grains inward. Using a non‐polymerizable analogue, we decouple chemical passivation from strain regulation, demonstrating compressive strain as the key factor enabling a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.53% for FAMA perovskite, alongside 98% efficiency retention after 1000 h of continuous illumination. Compatible with various additives and perovskite systems, this strategy delivers a champion PCE of 27.07% for CsFAMA triple‐cation devices, with a certified reverse‐scan efficiency of 26.81%. This establishes in situ polymerization as a foundational design principle for strain‐engineering perovskite semiconductors.

title: Single‐Atom Zn Interface Engineering for Efficient Noble‐Metal‐Free Photocatalytic Non‐Oxidative Coupling of Methane
content:
This work reports a noble‐metal‐free single‐atom photocatalyst, Zn─O─TiO2, for efficient photocatalytic non‐oxidative coupling of methane. Upon photoexcitation, the photogenerated electrons and holes separate and migrate to Zn and O sites, respectively, forming long‐lived Zn+ and O− reaction centers that drive H2 evolution and CH4 coupling.








ABSTRACT
ZnO‐based photocatalysts have attracted extensive attention for methane (CH4) conversion because their intrinsic internal electric field can effectively polarize and activate CH4. However, the mismatch between charge‐carrier dynamics and surface reaction kinetics limits the utilization of photogenerated reactive species, making noble‐metal modification necessary to achieve efficient methane conversion. In this study, we report a noble‐metal‐free single‐atom photocatalyst in which isolated Zn atoms are anchored onto anatase TiO2 via µ‐oxo bridges (Zn─O─TiO2) for photocatalytic non‐oxidative coupling of methane (NOCM). This structure not only promotes efficient charge separation and suppresses carrier recombination, enabling the formation of long‐lived Zn+ and O− reaction centers, but also provides active sites to accelerate surface reaction kinetics. Consequently, the catalyst achieves an ethane rate of 44.75 µmol·g−1·h−1 in a batch reactor, and 1.09 mmol·g−1·h−1 in a flow reactor. The apparent quantum efficiency reaches 8.81% at 350 nm. Mechanistic studies reveal that photogenerated holes at O− centers activate CH4 to CH3 radicals, while electrons at Zn+ sites drive H2 evolution, synergistically enabling efficient NOCM. This work establishes single‐atom interface engineering as an effective strategy for simultaneously promoting charge separation and enhancing surface catalytic reaction, providing a general strategy for designing noble‐metal‐free photocatalysts for small‐molecule activation.

title: Machine‐Learning‐Guided Polarization‐Lattice Decoupling Enables Ultrahigh Energy Storage in Lead‐Free Dielectric Ceramics
content:
An interpretable machine‐learning framework quantitatively links ionic descriptors with polarization behavior, enabling the discovery of a high‐polarization lead‐free dielectric composition. Coupled with viscous polymer processing, the designed ceramic achieves ultrahigh breakdown strength and energy density through polarization‐lattice decoupling, where nanoscale polarization clusters and multiphase coexistence enable reversible polarization rotation while suppressing long‐range ferroelectric order.








ABSTRACT
Achieving ultrahigh energy storage in lead‐free dielectric ceramics is fundamentally constrained by the intrinsic trade‐off between large polarization and high dielectric breakdown strength. Here, we establish an interpretable machine‐learning‐guided design framework that quantitatively links ionic descriptors with polarization behavior in ABO3‐based dielectric matrices, enabling the rational identification of compositions with intrinsically high polarization potential. Guided by this strategy, a (Bi0.275Na0.2255K0.0495Ba0.3)(Ti0.985Hf0.015)O3‐0.15(La0.5Sm0.5)2Ti2O7 (BNBT‐3) composition is discovered that exhibits an exceptional maximum polarization of 50.19 µC cm−2. When processed via a viscous polymer process, the resulting BNBT‐3‐VPP capacitors achieve an ultrahigh breakdown strength of 1400 kV cm−1 and a recoverable energy density of 25.1 J cm−3 with high efficiency, placing them among the best‐performing lead‐free dielectric ceramics reported to date. Structural characterization combined with phase‐field simulations reveals that the outstanding performance originates from polarization‐lattice decoupling, where nanoscale polarization clusters and multiphase coexistence suppress long‐range ferroelectric order while enabling reversible polarization rotation. This work establishes a generalizable strategy that integrates interpretable machine learning with physically grounded materials design, providing a powerful route for discovering high‐performance dielectric energy storage materials.

title: Solar‐Driven Spin‐State Optimization in Co‐Based Catalysts for Enhanced Photothermal Ammonia Synthesis
content:
The solar‐driven optimized Co‐based catalyst exhibited a remarkable catalytic activity enhancement, with its performance increased by 3 times compared to the thermal one. The plasmon‐induced hot electron enrichment on the catalyst surface regulated the spin state of active sites, driving their transformation toward a low‐spin state, which accounted for the significant improvement in catalytic performance.








ABSTRACT
Spin‐state engineering of active sites represents a key strategy for boosting catalytic performance, as demonstrated in thermal ammonia synthesis. However, conventional promoter‐mediated ground‐state spin modulation is inherently limited by the electronic structure of the catalyst, imposing a ceiling on achievable spin tuning efficacy and hindering further advances. In this work, we developed a series of cobalt (Co) nanoparticle‐based catalysts for photothermal ammonia synthesis. By introducing Ru single atom into the Co nanoparticles, along with the addition of barium as a promoter, spin‐state engineering of Co nanoparticles was optimized under light irradiation, boosting the production rate by 3 times compared to thermal catalytic conditions. In‐situ characterization studies revealed that the hot electrons accumulate on the catalyst surface and shift the Co active sites toward a lower‐spin configuration. Supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we demonstrate that this light‐induced spin state change modulates the electronic interaction between Co and N2, weakening the N≡N bond and lowering its dissociation energy barrier, thereby facilitating N2 activation. This work demonstrates that spin regulation in Co‐based catalysts is an innovative design principle for developing more efficient photothermal catalysts for ammonia synthesis and other applications.

title: Charge Confinement in an Ordered High‐Entropy Intermetallic Breaks the Activity‐Poisoning Trade‑Off for Glycolic Acid Electrosynthesis From Polyethylene Terephthalate
content:
An ordered high‐entropy intermetallic metallene creates a charge‐confined electronic environment through p–d orbital hybridization, enabling rapid ethylene glycol (EG) adsorption while weakening the binding of poisoning intermediates. This optimized adsorption–desorption balance breaks the activity–poisoning trade‐off and enables efficient, selective, and durable electrosynthesis of glycolic acid (GA) from polyethylene terephthalate hydrolysate under industrially relevant conditions.








ABSTRACT
Selective electrooxidation of ethylene glycol (EG) from polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolysate to glycolic acid (GA) offers a sustainable route for plastic upcycling but is hindered by insufficient activity at industrially relevant current densities and severe catalyst deactivation caused by poisoning intermediates. Here, we design a two‐dimensional ordered high‐entropy intermetallic, HEI (PdPtRh)(InBi)ene, based on a Pd1In1‐type body‐centered‐cubic framework. The ordered lattice induces pronounced p‐‐d hybridization and charge redistribution, giving rise to a charge‐confinement effect at the active sites. Operando infrared spectroscopy, CO stripping, and theoretical calculations reveal that this confined electronic environment precisely regulates the evolution of the key poisoning intermediate *COCH2OH, weakening its accumulation while preserving efficient EG activation. As a result, HEI (PdPtRh)(InBi)ene achieves a current density of 554.21 mA cm−2 at 0.9 V in PET hydrolysate (PETH). Furthermore, it maintains stable operation for 90 h in a flow cell at an industrially relevant current density of 200 mA cm−2, delivering an average GA Faradaic efficiency of 99.22% and an average GA production rate of 1.85 mmol h−1 cm−2. These findings demonstrate charge‐confinement engineering as an effective route to regulate poisoning‐intermediate behavior in electrocatalytic alcohol oxidation.

title: Spatially Synergistic Dual‐Confinement Enables Underwater‐Stable Room‐Temperature Phosphorescent Hydrogels
content:
An amphiphilic PVA‐assisted in situ curing process generates rigid luminescent epoxy microspheres within a densified PVA hydrogel network. The resulting spatially synergistic dual confinement restricts chromophore motion, suppresses water and oxygen ingress, and reinforces the hydrogel matrix, enabling ultralong room‐temperature phosphorescence, high afterglow luminance, mechanical robustness, and long‐term underwater stability.








ABSTRACT
Organic room‐temperature phosphorescent (RTP) hydrogels are attractive as flexible luminescent materials for optoelectronic and biomedical applications, but their water‐rich and mechanically compliant nature makes it difficult to create microenvironments that simultaneously suppress nonradiative decay, resist external quenching, and maintain structural robustness. Here, we report an amphiphilic polymer chain‐driven in situ curing strategy that generates rigid luminescent epoxy microspheres uniformly within a PVA hydrogel matrix. Combined with annealing–reswelling‐induced matrix densification, this process creates a spatially synergistic dual‐confinement system, in which the inner epoxy domains immobilize phosphors while the outer dense PVA network helps impede the ingress of water and oxygen. The resulting hydrogels exhibit tunable multicolor RTP, an ultralong phosphorescence lifetime of up to 4342 ms, a daylight‐visible afterglow luminance of 87.9 cd m−2, a time‐gated delayed‐emission quantum yield of 55.49%, and a tensile strength exceeding 10 MPa. Notably, the hydrogels retain a phosphorescence lifetime of 3172 ms after 170 days of water immersion. This work identifies spatially synergistic dual confinement as an effective route to jointly optimize phosphorescence efficiency, mechanical robustness, and long‐term underwater stability in soft luminescent hydrogels.

title: Covalently Anchored Multifunctional Interlayer Enables Ultrastable and Fast ‐ Charging Composite Solid ‐ State Sodium Metal Batteries
content:
A covalently anchored organosilane interlayer is constructed on ceramic particles through plasma activation and silane coupling. This multifunctional layer enhances particle dispersion, strengthens interface bonding, and regulates anion/solvent partitioning. The resulting composite electrolyte enables long‑life symmetric cells, high‑rate full cells, and flexible pouch batteries, all featuring a thin, uniform, NaF‑rich protection layer.








ABSTRACT
The practical application of composite solid‐state sodium metal batteries is critically limited by poor organic–inorganic compatibility, causing particle agglomeration, high interfacial resistance, and dendrite growth. Here, a covalent surface grafting strategy constructs a multifunctional interlayer covalently anchored on Na3Zr2Si2PO12, featuring a cross‑linked siloxane network and terminal ─NH2 groups. Covalent anchorage transforms inert particle surfaces into dispersible units, while ─NH2 groups anchor TFSI– and confine residual solvent via hydrogen bonding and Lewis acid‑base interactions. This dual regulation decouples ion transport from side reactions, yielding a high Na+ transference number (0.58) and a stable, NaF‑rich, thin solid‑electrolyte interphase (SEI). The optimized electrolyte enables symmetric cells with exceptional cycling stability and high critical current density (CCD). Full cells achieve fast‑charging (92 mAh g−1 at 15 C) and ultralong cycle life (76.4% retention after 7000 cycles at 10 C). A flexible pouch cell retains 97% capacity after 150 cycles. This work establishes that precise molecular‑level interfacial design, rather than simple physical blending, is key to high‑performance, dendrite‑resistant solid‑state sodium batteries.

title: Native Defects‐Induced Fermi‐Level Pinning and Diffuson‐Mediated Thermal Transport in BiSbSe3 Thermoelectrics
content:
Native Se vacancies and cation‐on‐Se antisites pin the Fermi level in BiSbSe3, stabilizing n‐type transport and hindering hole activation. Meanwhile, Sb‐centered lone‐pairs interactions soften low‐frequency optical phonons and promote diffuson‐mediated thermal transport. This defect‐vibration interplay explains the ultralow lattice thermal conductivity and identifies Fermi level depinning as the key to unlocking high‐performance p‐type thermoelectrics.








ABSTRACT
Ultralow thermal conductivity is widely recognized as a core characteristic of promising thermoelectrics, yet many such materials still fail to realize high thermoelectric performance. Te‐free BiSbSe3 embodies this contradiction: its intrinsically ultralow thermal conductivity makes it promising for medium‐temperature thermoelectric applications, while stable p‐type transport remains elusive and the optimization limits of both conduction types remain unclear. Here, we reveal that native defects and Sb containing lone‐pairs jointly govern its transport behavior. Electron microscopy analysis and first‐principles calculations confirm that Se vacancies and cation‐on‐Se antisite defects possess low formation enthalpies, stabilizing n‐type conduction, compensating holes, and pinning the Fermi level away from the valence band maximum. Moreover, strong near‐band‐edge Sb‐Se hybridization softens Sb‐dominated low‐frequency optical phonons, promoting acoustic‐optical coupling and diffuson‐like thermal transport at high temperatures. By matching theory and experiment, we identify carrier mobility degradation at high donor concentrations as the main limitation for n‐type BiSbSe3. Our calculations predict that eliminating Fermi‐level pinning could enable p‐type BiSbSe3 to achieve an excellent average ZT of ∼ 1.4 over 300‐800 K. These findings not only clarify the long‐standing underperformance of ultralow thermal conductivity thermoelectric compounds, but also establish a universal chemical design framework for optimizing Te‐free thermoelectrics.

title: Sodium Formate as a High‐Capacity Cathode Presodiation Additive for Ultra‐Stable Sodium‐Ion Batteries
content:
Catalyst‐free sodium formate as presodiation additive, with a higher HOMO energy level than carbonate solvents, preferentially oxidizes to suppress electrolyte decomposition. The released oxygen species promote the formation of a robust and thin CEI enriched with Na2O and COOR groups on the NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 cathode, synergistically reinforcing interfacial mechanical strength and electrochemical durability.








ABSTRACT
The initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) of sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) is substantially lower than that of lithium‐ion batteries, primarily owing to the intrinsic limitations of hard carbon anodes. Cathode sodium‐compensation additives have emerged as a promising strategy to address this challenge, offering both safety and ready scalability for mass production. However, most reported additives rely on catalytic decomposition, which inevitably raises cost and introduces inert components into the battery. Here, catalyst‐free sodium formate (HCOONa) is introduced as a cathode additive that delivers a sodium‐compensation capacity of 398 mAh g−1. It is revealed that the HCOO− possesses a higher highest occupied molecular orbital energy than conventional carbonate solvents, enabling preferential oxidation that suppresses detrimental electrolyte decomposition. The oxygen species derived from HCOONa facilitate the formation of a robust and thin cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) on the NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 cathode. This CEI comprises a Na2O‐rich inorganic phase and a COOR‐rich organic phase, which enhance interfacial mechanical strength and electrochemical stability. Hard carbon||NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 pouch cells containing 2.5 wt% HCOONa exhibit a 5.7% increased initial discharge capacity and superior cycling stability, retaining 88% capacity after 700 cycles. These findings establish an effective presodiation strategy that compensates for sodium loss while stabilizing electrode interfaces in practical SIBs.

title: Discovery of Multicomponent Invar Materials With Low Thermal Expansion, High Curie Temperature, and Superior Phase Stability Assisted by Active Learning
content:
An interpretable active‐learning framework navigates a multicomponent Fe─Co─Ni─Cr─Mn space to identify and experimentally refine a productive low‐thermal‐expansion basin. The resulting FCC Invar alloy combines near‐zero expansion over a broad temperature range with a Curie temperature of about 580 K and good ductility, demonstrating a property‐first route to accelerated alloy discovery.








ABSTRACT
Zero thermal expansion (ZTE) materials provide exceptional dimensional stability under temperature fluctuations, making them indispensable for high‐precision instrumentation and extreme environments. However, their natural scarcity, combined with the vast compositional space in multicomponent systems, renders traditional trial‐and‐error approaches both time‐consuming and cost‐prohibitive, posing an emergent challenge for modern high‐tech applications. Here, we establish a task‐specific active‐learning framework with empirical fine‐tuning to accelerate ZTE materials' design. By mining sparse experimental datasets, we identified a high‐potential compositional region and uncovered several novel low‐expansion alloys. Among them, Cr1.4Co8.9Ni30.5Fe59 exhibits a low coefficient of thermal expansion of 1.9±0.3×10−6K−1$1.9 \pm 0.3\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K}^{-1}$, and a high Curie temperature reaching 580 K$\mathrm{K}$. Real‐time in situ neutron and synchrotron x‐ray diffraction confirm its single‐phase face‐centered cubic structure, excellent ductility, and robust phase stability against thermal and mechanical stimuli. Crucially, machine learning analysis pinpointed six key descriptors highly correlated with low‐expansion performance, providing data‐driven insights into the magnetovolume origins of this behavior. This work not only yields a high‐performance dimensionally stable alloy, but also demonstrates how integrating physical insights with data‐driven design can accelerate advanced materials development.

title: Glucose‐Derived Circular Thermoset Platform Breaks the Industrial Trilemma of Recyclable Structural Polymers
content:
A catalyst‐ and solvent‐free one‐pot strategy transforms three industrial feedstocks into glucose‐derived dynamic thermosets that combine long shelf life, rapid curing, compatibility with industrial vacuum‐assisted resin infusion, and a tensile strength of 113 MPa. Room‐temperature closed‐loop recycling recovers carbon fibers without performance loss and upcycles matrix products into epoxy curing agents.








ABSTRACT
The long‐standing trilemma of scalable green synthesis, industrial processing compatibility, and balanced performance‐circularity represents the core barrier limiting real‐world deployment of recyclable thermosets. Here, we report an exogenous catalyst‐ and solvent‐free one‐pot strategy with ∼100% atom economy to fabricate glucose‐derived built‐in dynamic covalent thermosets from three industrial bulk feedstocks: glucose, maleic anhydride, and pentaerythritol tetrakis(3‐mercaptopropionate). The optimal formulation achieves an unprecedented balance between >130 d of room‐temperature shelf life (no gelation) and 2‐min gelation at 150°C, delivering engineering‐grade tensile strength up to 113 MPa, 17.5 MPa steel lap shear strength, and drop‐in compatibility with industrial vacuum‐assisted resin infusion for large carbon fiber composite manufacturing. We demonstrate complete room‐temperature closed‐loop recycling: nondestructive recovery of high‐value carbon fibers with full performance retention, and matrix degradation products (73.2%–83.1% isolated yield) upcyclable into high‐performance epoxy curing agents. Thermal reprocessing provides an additional reuse pathway for manufacturing scrap. Our cradle‐to‐grave life cycle assessment confirms 81.4% lower CO2‐equivalent emissions than virgin bisphenol A epoxy carbon fiber composites. This work establishes a generalizable, industrially deployable paradigm for circular high‐performance thermosets, resolving the long‐standing trilemma impeding recyclable thermosets deployment.

title: 3D Cuprous Iodide Cluster‐Covalent Organic Framework for Ultrasensitive and Highly Selective Trace HF Detection at Room Temperature
content:
A diamond‐topology CuI cluster‐based covalent organic framework (CuI‐MCOF) is reported that enables ultrafast, highly sensitive, and anti‐interference HF gas recognition through synergistic CuI‐cluster/imine‐linker interactions. Moreover, CuI‐MCOF is integrated into an on‐chip miniaturized perceptron system for ppb‐level HF discrimination, spatiotemporal distribution estimation, and leakage‐source prediction.








ABSTRACT
Hydrofluoric acid (HF) poses a serious and irreversible threat to human health necessitating the development of highly sensitive and selective detection materials. Herein, a three‐dimensional cuprous iodide cluster‐based covalent organic framework (CuI‐MCOF), with diamond topology has been successfully prepared, which shows an ultrafast and highly sensitive response to HF gas. At room temperature, CuI‐MCOF displays an exceptional response of 7188% toward 100 ppm HF, with remarkably rapid response/recovery times of 3 s/2 s at 4 ppm. Notably, the sensor achieves an ultralow detection limit of 21 ppb, outperforming previously reported HF sensors. Moreover, it demonstrates outstanding selectivity and anti‐interference performance, maintaining stable responses to 4 ppm HF even in the presence of 16 interfering gases (100 ppm each). Experiments combined with density‐functional theory calculations reveal that the imine‐linker N atoms serve as reversible HF adsorption–desorption sites, while the electron‐rich CuI clusters enhance dipole interactions and facilitate charge transfer. Leveraging these properties, an on‐chip miniaturized perceptron system integrated with evaluation algorithms is developed for anti‐interference HF discrimination, spatiotemporal distribution estimation, and leakage source prediction. This work provides a new strategy for designing high‐performance HF sensors and expands the application of cluster‐based COFs in gas sensing.

title: Bacteria‐Trained, MnO2‐Armored Dendritic Cells for Immunotherapy
content:
MnO2‐armored, bacteria‐trained dendritic cells undergo tumor‐responsive mechanical and immunological transformation. The nanocoating masks immune ligands and maintains a mechanically stiff, quiescent state during circulation, while the tumor microenvironment removes the armor and restores cellular deformability and immune accessibility. This dynamic transition promotes tumor infiltration, lymph node trafficking, and localized immune activation for effective cancer therapy.








ABSTRACT
Precise control over the phenotypic state of immune cells is critical for overcoming the limitations of on‐target off‐tumor toxicity and inefficient tumor infiltration in cell‐based cancer immunotherapy. Here, we developed an engineered DC platform—trained with inactivated bacteria and armored with MnO2 nanoparticles (designated MnArmL‐trDCs)—endowed with immune reconfigurability and mechano‐transformable characteristics to boost tumor penetration and remodel immune microenvironment. In circulation, the MnO2 armor enforces a stiff mechanical state and globally masks surface immunological ligands (such as CD80, CD86, MHC‐II, and CCR7), rendering the DCs biologically silent and resistant to premature immune recognition or hepatic clearance. These engineered cells integrate selectively into lesion sites, enabling restoration of the deformability of dendritic cells and targeted intratumoral immune activation triggered by local pH and hydrogen peroxide. This transformation enables deep tumor penetration, robust activation of TLR, NLR, and cGAS‐STING pathways, and efficient trafficking to tumor‐draining lymph nodes. In vivo, MnArmL‐trDCs induce a pro‐inflammatory immune landscape, promote cytotoxic lymphocyte infiltration, reverse immunosuppression, and synergize with anti‐PD‐1 therapy to achieve sustained tumor regression. This nano‐engineering cell armor‐based strategy could also be possibly expanded to different cell types in other types of immunotherapies.

title: In Situ Polymerization of Covalent Organic Frameworks Networks for Efficient and Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
A synergistic assembly strategy (SAS) introduces COF monomers separately into perovskite precursor and antisolvent, enabling in situ polymerization at grain boundaries of perovskite. This approach effectively regulates crystallization of perovskite, passivates ionic defects, and enhances hydrophobicity of the perovskite film. Consequently, record‐high efficiency of 26.74% among COF‐based inverted PSCs is achieved, along with outstanding long‐term stability under heat, humidity, and continuous light.








ABSTRACT
The crystallization quality and defect density of perovskite films are key factors determining the performance and lifetime of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Moreover, covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as highly promising multifunctional passivators for PSCs due to their abundant functional groups, periodic pore channels, and excellent chemical stability. However, the strong π–π stacking interactions resulting from the inherently rigid aromatic backbone of COFs lead to extremely poor dispersibility in conventional solvents, severely limiting further improvements in their passivation efficiency and device performance. In response to this issue, we propose a COF‐based synergistic assembly strategy (SAS): introducing two monomers into the perovskite precursor solution and the antisolvent, respectively, to form a COF network via in situ polymerization at grain boundaries during the annealing process. This design not only avoids the agglomeration issues associated with pre‐synthesized COFs, but also effectively regulates crystallization kinetics, passivates defects, suppresses ion migration, and enhances the film's hydrophobicity through the synergistic effects of hydrogen bonding and coordination. The SAS‐treated PSCs achieve a high power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.74% and excellent long‐term stability. This strategy provides a new approach to material design for achieving high efficiency and stability in PSCs.

title: Photothermal Catalytic Dry Reforming of Methane With 1000‐Hour Stability via Redox Shuttle of Metal Vanadate
content:
A Rh/Mg2V1.33O4 catalyst was developed for ultra‐stable photothermal catalytic DRM. The quasi‐metallic defective spinel vanadate enables full‐spectrum solar harvesting and efficient photothermal conversion. During operation, the interfacial redox shuttle (Rhδ+─Ov─Vn+ ⇌ Rhδ+─Ol─V(n+1)+) enables efficient Ol migration and dynamic regeneration, steering the reaction along a coking‐resistant CH3O* pathway and ensuring structural stability. A 1000‐h long‐term stability with only trace coke formation was achieved.








ABSTRACT
Photothermal catalytic dry reforming of methane (DRM) mediated by lattice oxygen (Ol) is promising for converting two major greenhouse gases into syngas. However, conventional oxide supports possess strong metal–oxygen bonds that restrict Ol migration, compromising stability, typically less than 200 h. Herein, we design a Rh/Mg2V1.33O4 catalyst with Rhδ+─Ov─Vn+ interfacial sites (n = 3 or 4). The defective spinel vanadate support exhibits quasi‐metallic properties, enabling efficient solar harvesting and photothermal conversion. Under 4 W cm−2 light irradiation without external heating, the redox flexibility of V species enables an interfacial redox shuttle (Rhδ+─Ov─Vn+ ⇌ Rhδ+─Ol─V(n+1)+), which endows the catalyst with effective Ol migration and regeneration ability in the DRM reaction. This property steers the reaction along a coking‐resistant CH3O* pathway and guarantees structural stability. As a result, the catalyst delivers long‐term stability for 1000 h, outperforming state‐of‐the‐art photothermal catalysts. It also achieves high syngas generation rates of 16.1 and 18.6 mol gRh−1 h−1 for H2 and CO, respectively, along with a light‐to‐chemical energy efficiency of ∼20.9%. This work establishes quasi‐metallic, redox‐active vanadate supports as a transformative platform for durable Ol‐mediated photothermal catalysis.

title: Processing Window Expansion Enables Uniform Crystallization in Scalable Ambient‐Fabricated Perovskite Photovoltaics
content:
The combined additive (CA) strategy is developed for ambient slot‐die coating to modulate nucleation and phase evolution, suppressing the undesirable δ‐phase formation and reducing lattice strain. This approach enables an efficiency of 22.70% for a perovskite solar module, and the unencapsulated device retains 97.76% of initial efficiency after 1300 h under ISOS‐L‐3.








ABSTRACT
Slot‐die coating is a promising scalable deposition technique for perovskite devices due to its high material utilization and inherent compatibility with continuous manufacturing. However, a narrow deposition‐to‐annealing time window and inhomogeneous ink distribution limit the device performance. Herein, we report a combined additive (CA) strategy that simultaneously regulates nucleation kinetics and phase evolution, broadening the processing window for slot‐die coating in the ambient. By synergistically introducing rubidium thiocyanate (RbSCN) and formamidinium thiocyanate (FASCN), an in situ coordination mechanism is established that lowers the energy barrier for the δ‐to‐α phase transition while suppressing non‐photoactive phase formation. This leads to uniform crystallization over an extended time window exceeding 100 s, yielding dense large‐grained α‐FAPbI3 films with minimized vertical compositional gradient and reduced residual strain. The resulting films exhibit suppressed defects, prolonged carrier lifetime, and optimized energy‐level alignment, enabling efficient charge extraction and reduced nonradiative recombination. The CA strategy enables highly uniform large‐area deposition to deliver an efficiency of 22.70% for perovskite solar modules. Meanwhile, the unencapsulated devices maintain 97.76% of the initial efficiency under ISOS‐L‐3 for 1300 h. This CA strategy establishes a generalizable pathway for decoupling crystallization kinetics from processing constraints, providing a robust method for scalable high‐performance perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Nanocatalytic Inhibition of ROS‐Dependent GSDMD Palmitoylation Mitigates Sepsis Progression
content:
This work unveils enhanced Gasdermin D (GSDMD) palmitoylation in periphreal blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from sepsis patients, a process orchestrated by reactive oxygen species (ROS) and ZDHHC5/9. Leveraging this mechanistic insight, VOOH nanocatalysts are rationally designed and screened to serve dual roles as ROS scavengers and GSDMD palmitoylation inhibitors, with lattice plane optimization enabling effective blockade of pyroptosis and inflammation, thereby conferring therapeutic benefits in sepsis models.








ABSTRACT
Sepsis is a life‐threatening condition characterized by multiple organ dysfunction, high morbidity, and mortality. Gasdermin D (GSDMD)‐mediated pyroptosis constitutes a key pathogenic mechanism. Here, we discovered that GSDMD in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from septic patients undergoes enhanced palmitoylation, driven by reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mediated by ZDHHC5/ZDHHC9 transferases. Targeting this new mechanism, we designed and screened vanadium oxide hydroxide nanosheets (VOOH NSs) as catalytic ROS scavengers and GSDMD palmitoylation inhibitor. Crucially, we investigated and optimized the exposure patterns of specific lattice planes to maximize their ROS‐eliminating capability. This intervention measure prevents GSDMD palmitoylation, inhibits both canonical and non‐canonical pyroptosis, alleviates inflammatory damage, and demonstrates potent therapeutic effects in two sepsis animal models. Validation in GSDMD‐knockout mice further confirms this palmitoylation pathway as the key therapeutic target. These results demonstrate that targeting ROS‐mediated GSDMD palmitoylation is a key therapeutic strategy for treating sepsis.

title: Threo‐Chiral Cation Additive Enables Ordered Lattice Adsorption and Enhanced Operational Stability of Perovskite Photovoltaics
content:
The threo‐chiral cation additive was developed to lower lattice surface energy, steer preferential (100) crystal orientation, and suppress lattice distortion as well as ion migration through a distinct stereoselective “lock‐and‐key” interaction. The devices and modules achieved champion power conversion efficiencies of 26.68% (certified 26.31%) and 22.78% (certified 22.12%), respectively. Moreover, unencapsulated devices demonstrated superior thermal and long‐term operational stabilities.








ABSTRACT
Chiral molecular engineering is an effective strategy to modulate crystallization and mitigate nonradiative defects in perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, unconstrained bond rotation often leads to spatial mismatch between chiral molecules and the perovskite lattice, hindering effective defect coordination. Herein, we introduce threo‐chiral cation additive of (2S,3R)‐2‐amino‐3‐hydroxybutanamide hydrochloride (ThrA) to achieve precise perovskite lattice regulation. Benefiting from methyl‑induced steric hindrance originating from its dual chiral‑center threo‑configuration, ThrA acquires a conformationally locked rigid stereostructure and further facilitates thermodynamically‑favored parallel‑to‑lattice multi‑site synergistic adsorption via hydrogen bonding and Pb coordination. Such stereoselective “lock‐and‐key” interaction reduces lattice surface energy, guides preferential (100) crystal growth, and simultaneously suppresses lattice distortion and ion migration. Consequently, the ThrA‐modified inverted PSCs achieve a champion efficiency of 26.68% (certified 26.31%), while 65 cm2 large‐area module delivers a promising PCE of 22.78% (certified 22.12%), representing one of the outstanding certification efficiencies for perovskite modules of comparable size. Unencapsulated devices retain 90% of their initial efficiency after 1000 h thermal aging (ISOS‐D‐2) and maintain 92% performance after 2000 h continuous maximum power point tracking (ISOS‐L‐2). This work demonstrates that the stereostructure of additive is decisive for precise perovskite crystallization modulation, providing advanced stereochemical strategy toward high‐efficiency and ultra‐stable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Monolithically 3D‐Printed Spectral‐Spatial Meta‐Authenticators
content:
A single height map printed in a low‐index resin by two‐photon lithography encodes multiple visible wavelengths in one metasurface without any polarization optics. A fabrication‐aware optimization folds the printable height levels into the design, so the device is printed as optimized. It reconstructs a publicly readable far‐field key together with wavelength‐ and distance‐locked near‐field passwords for dual‐credential optical authentication.








ABSTRACT
Metasurface holography can encode multiple independent images in a single flat element, yet simultaneous operation at several visible wavelengths has typically relied on geometric‐phase elements, which require a prescribed circular polarization and bulky polarization optics, and on high‐index dielectrics that can suffer from visible‐band absorption. Here, we demonstrate a monolithically 3D‐printed, low‐index, height‐coded metasurface that performs polarization‐insensitive, broadband holography across spectral (wavelength) and spatial (near‐ and far‐field) channels. The propagation phase accumulated by each resin pillar is set by its height, so a single height map fixes the phase response at every wavelength at once and acts as a multi‐wavelength phase library. The symmetric pillar cross‐section removes the dependence on input polarization, and the transparent resin keeps the response low‐loss across the visible band. A fabrication‐aware optimization folds the discrete height levels imposed by two‐photon‐lithography slicing directly into the loss, so the design is printed as optimized in a single continuous step, without post‐optimization rounding. Experimentally, the device reconstructs a far‐field image that is read directly as a public key together with wavelength‐ and distance‐selective near‐field images that act as locked passwords, realizing a compact, dual‐credential optical authentication scheme under unpolarized illumination without polarization optics.

title: Spin‐State Modulation of Octahedral Co Sites for Enhancing Nitrate‐to‐Ammonia Conversion
content:
Metal–organic framework‐derived Co3O4 (MD‐Co3O4) features oxygen‐vacancies that selectively reconstruct octahedral cobalt (CoOh) sites into an electron‐rich, high‐spin state. The resulting CoOh centers strengthen nitrate adsorption and accelerate its conversion to ammonia, delivering a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 96.7% along with superior stability and broad applicability.








ABSTRACT
Ammonia is vital for agriculture and a promising carbon‐free energy carrier, but its industrial production via the Haber–Bosch process is energy‐intensive and emits substantial CO2. Electrocatalytic nitrogen oxide reduction to ammonia offers a green alternative, by using renewable electricity under ambient conditions while enabling nitrogen resource utilization. Herein, we report a metal–organic framework (MOF)‐derived Co3O4 electrocatalyst (MD‐Co3O4) prepared by controlled pyrolysis of Co‐MOF‐74, which achieved a high Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 96.7% and excellent stability for the electrosynthesis of NH3 from nitrate, along with robust activity over a wide pH and nitrate concentration range. Comprehensive spectroscopic characterizations and density functional theory calculations revealed that the oxygen vacancies generated during MOF pyrolysis induce coordination distortion of octahedral Co sites, leading to a high‐spin state transition with an electron‐rich configuration that synergistically enhances nitrate adsorption and interfacial electron transfer, thereby boosting the intrinsic activity. Moreover, this MOF‐based strategy is applicable to other M1Co2O4 spinels, which provides an effective approach for spin engineering at the atomic scale and sustainable ammonia synthesis.

title: Heterointerfacial Bonding Governs Service Stability in Flexible Perovskite Photovoltaics
content:
An active energy‐dissipating multi‐bond network, constructed by blending polyamide curing agents with fullerene derivatives, enhances interfacial adhesion in flexible perovskite solar modules. This strategy yields a 100 cm2 module with 22.33% efficiency. In situ bending electroluminescence tests confirm exceptional service stability, showing no significant performance decline after 5000 cycles under ultraviolet irradiation and mechanical stress.








ABSTRACT
The service stability of flexible perovskite solar module (FPSM) is contingent upon the bonding strength and stress‐response behavior at heterointerfaces. However, the fullerene‐based layer mainly relies on weak non‐covalent interactions. This makes it difficult for the FPSM to tackle the challenges posed by the coupling of multiple stresses in the actual service environment. Through the blending strategy of the polyamide curing agent and fullerene derivatives, we constructed an active energy‐dissipating multi‐bond network featuring covalent bond anchoring and hydrogen bond dissipation, which significantly enhanced the interfacial bonding and energy dissipation capabilities. Based on this strategy, a 100 cm2 FPSM achieves a recorded power conversion efficiency of 22.33% (certified 21.5%). More importantly, for the first time, we developed an in situ bending electroluminescence experiment for FPSM under ultraviolet irradiation. After 5000 consecutive bending cycles, there was no significant decline in the module's performance, which verified its service stability under multi‐field coupling.

title: Activation‐Free and Strain‐Resilient Island‐Bridge Liquid Metal Inks for Machine‐Learning‐Enabled Epidermal Electromyography
content:
A CuCNTs/LMPs island‐bridge architecture enables intrinsically conductive, activation‐free liquid‐metal inks with high‐resolution printability and strong electromechanical resilience. The printed conductors retain a sheet resistance of 1.3 × 10−1 Ω sq−1 at 300% strain and integrate into breathable 12‐channel HD‐sEMG arrays, enabling machine‐learning‐assisted load classification and continuous monitoring of fatigue‐associated exercise states during dynamic exercise.








ABSTRACT
Liquid metal particle‐based inks offer a scalable route toward stretchable electronics, yet their practical implementation is hindered by activation‐dependent conductivity and poor electrical stability under deformation. Herein, we report an intrinsically conductive and strain‐resilient liquid metal ink with a rationally engineered island‐bridge micro‐architecture, in which Cu‐decorated carbon nanotubes (CuCNTs) bridge adjacent liquid metal particles (LMPs) through initial hydrogen‐bonding/coordination‐assisted attachment to the native gallium‐oxide shell, followed by local Cu‐Ga alloying at the CuCNTs/LMPs interface. Enabled by solvent‐mediated dispersion and interfacial hybridization, the strain‐resilient composite ink supports high‐resolution (100 µm) screen printing and deformable circuit integration. The dynamically reconfigurable island‐bridge network retains a sheet resistance of 1.3 × 10−1 Ω sq−1 at 300% strain, together with stable resistance during prolonged cyclic stretching and bending. When printed into a compact 12‐channel array on breathable fibrous substrates, the resulting electrode array exhibits low skin‐electrode impedance and superior high‐density surface electromyography (HD‐sEMG) performance compared with commercial gel electrodes. Combined with machine‐learning‐assisted analysis, the electromyography arrays enable training‐state recognition, individualized load assessment, and continuous monitoring of fatigue‐associated exercise states during dynamic exercise. This work provides a scalable strategy for intrinsically conductive liquid metal electronics and advances their application in intelligent wearable biointerfaces and soft electronic systems.

title: Adaptive Supramolecular Interactions Govern Redox‐Active Molecules in Aqueous Redox Flow Batteries
content:
Adaptive supramolecular interactions overcome the solubility‐stability trade‐off in aqueous redox flow batteries. Hydrophobic anions disrupt intrinsic π–π stacking to enable high solubility, while redox‐state‐dependent spin pairing and cation coordination dynamically stabilize reactive intermediates during operation. This reversible structural evolution suppresses degradation, unlocking highly reversible energy storage over one thousand cycles.








ABSTRACT
Weak noncovalent interactions critically govern molecular behavior in solution, yet how they shape redox processes in aqueous electrochemical environments remains underexplored. Here, we demonstrate control over the solubility and redox stability of aromatic redox‐active molecules in aqueous redox flow batteries (RFBs). Zwitterionic substitution of naphthalene diimide (NDI) bearing quaternary ammonium and sulfonate groups shows weak π–π cohesion through steric and electrostatic effects, rendering otherwise insoluble NDIs responsive to external anions. Hydrophobic and weakly hydrated anions such as iodide and bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide disrupt residual stacking through anion–π interactions, enabling dissolution to concentrations approaching 1.3 M. Upon electrochemical reduction, these anions dissociate, and the reduced NDI species are instead stabilized through spin pairing and cation‐mediated intermolecular interactions, which suppress irreversible aggregation, slow self‐discharge, and enable rapid redox reactions. Operando Raman spectroscopy, 1H NMR, and EPR elucidate the redox‐state‐dependent evolution of these supramolecular assemblies. Together, these results establish zwitterionic molecular design for adaptive supramolecular redox chemistry in aqueous RFBs.

title: Time‐Encoded Ligand Presentation via a Magnetically Actuated Hydrogel Mitigates T Cell Exhaustion
content:
A magnetically actuated, extracellular matrix–mimetic hydrogel dynamically exposes or conceals T‐cell stimulatory ligands, enabling programmable alternation between activation and rest. This time‐encoded presentation attenuates proximal TCR signaling during rest phases, limits exhaustion‐associated programming, enriches central memory–like CD8+ T cells, and improves antigen‐specific cytotoxicity and tumor control, offering a non‐genetic strategy for T‐cell manufacturing.








ABSTRACT
Adoptive T cell therapy (ACT) requires ex vivo expansion of tumor‐reactive CD8+ T cells, yet prolonged antigenic stimulation frequently induces exhaustion, limiting persistence and therapeutic efficacy. Here, we present a magnetically actuated, extracellular matrix–mimetic hydrogel that enables reversible control of T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation timing. By embedding αCD3ε/αCD28‐functionalized magnetic nanoparticles within a soft hyaluronic acid matrix, external magnetic fields dynamically expose or conceal stimulatory ligands, allowing programmable alternation between activation and rest. Continuous ligand presentation sustains TCR signaling and drives inhibitory receptor expression and functional exhaustion. In contrast, alternating activation–rest cycles periodically attenuate proximal TCR signaling, reduce exhaustion‐associated marker expression, and bias differentiation toward central memory‐like states while preserving cytokine production and recall capacity. T cells expanded under intermittent stimulation exhibit enhanced antigen‐specific cytotoxicity, reduced dependence on PD‐1 blockade, and superior tumor control in vivo, together with increased CD8+ T cell abundance across analyzed tissues. These results identify temporal control of mechanochemical signaling as a materials‐encoded regulator of T cell fate and provide a non‐genetic strategy for generating functionally competent T cell products with reduced exhaustion‐associated dysfunction and improved antitumor activity.

title: Programmable Engineered Living Vehicles as Autonomous Biofactories for Synergistic Osteomyelitis Management and Bone Regeneration
content:
A programmable engineered living vehicle (ELV) is developed as an intelligent bio‐hybrid autonomous living biofactory for the synergistic management of multidrug‐resistant osteomyelitis. Guided by a bone‐homing navigation module, this synthetic living matter actively penetrates recalcitrant biofilms and autonomously executes temperature‐dependent therapeutic biomanufacturing, simultaneously achieving precise pathogen eradication and accelerated bone tissue regeneration.








ABSTRACT
Conventional static biomaterials and synthetic nanomedicines struggle to penetrate recalcitrant biofilms and orchestrate tissue regeneration in deep‐seated infections due to limited autonomous navigation and a lack of spatiotemporal responsiveness. Here, we conceptualize and develop a programmable engineered living vehicle (ELV) that functions as an autonomous biofactory for the synergistic management of drug‐resistant osteomyelitis. Built upon a self‐propelled Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 chassis with innate ecological dominance, these living biofactories are hierarchically equipped with environmental biosensors and logic‐gated computing modules. Crucially, leveraging AlphaFold 3‐guided molecular docking, we engineered multiscale thermo‐responsive genetic logic circuits that enable precise, temperature‐dependent biomanufacturing of bacteriolytic lysostaphin (LYS) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (≥37°C), coupled with a fail‐safe thermal self‐destruct mechanism (≥42°C). Furthermore, surface‐engineered (DSS)6 peptides confer robust hydroxyapatite affinity, acting as a bone‐homing navigation module. In a rat osteomyelitis model induced by methicillin‐resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), intravenously deployed ELV biofactories autonomously navigate to the infected niche, actively penetrate biofilms, and outperform vancomycin in pathogen clearance. Concurrently, localized payload secretion reprograms the osteo‐immune microenvironment, significantly accelerating bone repair. This work establishes a versatile paradigm for next‐generation smart living therapeutics, bridging synthetic biology with micro‐engineering to address complex clinical challenges.

title: Lewis‐Basic Metal Sulfide Electrode Interfaces Unlock High Power Density Alkaline All‐Iron Redox Flow Batteries
content:
Sluggish outer‐sphere electron transfer of Fe‐chelate anolytes is revealed as the hidden kinetic bottleneck in alkaline all‐iron redox flow batteries. Lewis‐basic Ni3S4 interfaces unlock rapid redox kinetics by increasing OHP‐region accessibility and strengthening interfacial electronic coupling, enabling a peak power density of 501.2 mW cm−2, an average energy efficiency of 77.8%, and stable 3000‐cycles operation at 200 mA cm−2.








ABSTRACT
Alkaline all‐iron redox flow batteries (AIRFBs) are promising for safe, low‐cost grid‐scale energy storage using Earth‐abundant elements. However, insufficient energy efficiency and power density limit practical deployment, while the interfacial kinetic origin of these losses remains unclear. Here, we identify sluggish outer‐sphere electron‐transfer kinetics of Fe‐chelate anolytes as a key kinetic bottleneck governing polarization in alkaline AIRFBs and further link this bottleneck to limited outer Helmholtz plane (OHP)‐region accessibility and weak interfacial electronic coupling. To overcome this limitation, we develop Lewis‐basic sulfide interfaces that regulate the local Fe‐chelate/electrode environment. These regulated interfaces convert inefficient diffusion encounters into productive sulfide‐assisted outer‐sphere electron‐transfer events, thereby accelerating anolyte redox kinetics and suppressing polarization. An alkaline AIRFB assembled with a Ni3S4‐modified electrode delivers an energy efficiency of 80.65% at 200 mA cm−2 and a peak power density of 501.2 mW cm−2, compared with 65.69% and 185.5 mW cm−2 for the pristine cell. The Ni3S4‐based cell further maintains an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.9%, an average energy efficiency of 77.8%, and stable operation over 3000 cycles at 200 mA cm−2. This work reveals an interfacial kinetic bottleneck in alkaline AIRFBs and establishes Lewis‐basic interface engineering as a strategy for high‐power and low‐cost long‐duration energy storage.

title: Intermolecular Interaction Engineering for Efficient Large‐Area Tin‐based Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
Molecular engineering of poly(3,4‐ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) with the p‐type small molecule FEG establishes strong intermolecular interactions that regulate polymer microstructure, acidity and interfacial properties. This enables high‐quality Sn‐based perovskite films and efficient, stable solar cells, achieving 17.02% efficiency for small‐area devices and 14.92% for 1‐cm2 devices.








ABSTRACT
Poly(3,4‐ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS) has been widely used as a hole transport layer (HTL) in environmentally friendly tin‐based perovskite solar cells (TPSCs). However, its intrinsic weak acidity and strong tendency toward molecular aggregates hinder its performance in TPSCs. Here, we develop a molecular engineering strategy by introducing a p‐type small molecule, 4,4'‐(5,6‐bis(2‐methoxyethoxy)benzo[c][1,2,5]thiadiazole‐4,7‐diyl)bis(2,5‐difluoro‐N,N‐bis(4‐methoxyphenyl)aniline) (FEG), to modify PEDOT:PSS and, crucially, employ a comprehensive set of solid‐state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) techniques to directly elucidate the intermolecular interactions governing this modification. Magic‐angle spinning 1H NMR, 1H‐1H double‐quantum‐single‐quantum correlation spectroscopy, and variable spinning‐rate measurements reveal strong interactions between FEG and PSS that redistribute the PEDOT:PSS microstructure and promote greater charge delocalization within the conductive polymer network. This interaction improves PEDOT:PSS dispersion, neutralizes residual acidity and enhances interfacial wettability, enabling the growth of high‐quality Sn‐based perovskite films with enlarged grains, reduced defect density and relieved residual stress. As a result, trap‐assisted recombination is suppressed and hole extraction is improved. Consequently, FEG‐PEDOT:PSS‐based TPSCs achieve a record efficiency of 14.92% for 1‐cm2 devices and a champion efficiency of 17.02% for 0.04‐cm2 devices, substantially outperforming their pristine PEDOT counterparts. Furthermore, these devices exhibit excellent operational stability, maintaining over 85% of their initial efficiency after 1100 h of storage under a N2 atmosphere.

title: A Precursor Design Principle for Archipelagic Hard‐Carbon Structural Evolution Through Cohesion–Solvation Regulation of Asphaltene Molecular Heterogeneity
content:
Solvent fractionation tunes the balance between intermolecular cohesion and solvation in asphaltene precursors, directing their conversion into archipelagic hard carbon. Selective retention of aromatic cores and oxidative stabilization promote separated carbon domains and confined pores. This precursor design enables reversible sodium storage with high capacity and rate capability while maintaining 92.3% capacity retention after 10 000 cycles.








ABSTRACT
Sodium‐ion batteries are central to the development of affordable electrochemical storage for renewable energy integration. Yet hard‐carbon anode design lacks a precursor‐level principle linking molecular assembly in chemically heterogeneous feedstocks to oxidative stabilization and closed‐pore formation. Here we establish a precursor‐level cohesion‐solvation design principle for regulating molecular selection and assembly in heterogeneous aromatic feedstocks. Toluene‐fractionated asphaltene precursors undergo oxidative crosslinking, redirecting carbonization from continuous coke‐like growth toward separated turbostratic domains and confined closed pores. A hard‐carbon performance screening index (HPSI) quantifies structural and electrochemical performance, while density functional theory (DFT) reveals stronger Na affinity and lower migration barriers in defect‐engineered carbon galleries. The solvent‐selected AHC‐80‐1400 delivers 400.1 mAh g−1 at 0.05 A g−1 with 87.7% ICE and retains 92.3% capacity after 10 000 cycles, while sustaining wide‐temperature sodium storage with 91.8% and 90.4% retention at −20°C and 50°C, respectively. At scale, a 10‐kg batch enables a 1.18 Ah NFM||AHC‐80‐1400 pouch cell, delivering 163.3 Wh kg−1 and 95.5% retention after 700 cycles. A cradle‐to‐gate life‐cycle assessment (LCA) shows that AHC‐80‐1400 production reduces climate‐change impact by 33.7% relative to Commercial HC. These findings establish precursor‐stage molecular selection as a design principle for harnessing feedstock heterogeneity to control carbonization trajectories and electrochemical function.

title: Stabilizing Ru Sites via Lattice Oxygen Locking of Nb‐Ru/RuO2 to Break the Activity–Stability Trade‐Off for Acidic Oxygen Evolution
content:
The Nb‐doped Ru/RuO2 heterostructure catalyst is designed to inhibit the unstable LOM and concurrently to propose a favorable Brønsted Site‐Promoted Proton Transfer (BSPT) mechanism derived from the AEM. This design effectively lowers the deprotonation energy barrier and breaks the conventional scaling relations, thereby achieving substantial improvements in activity and stability.








ABSTRACT
Developing highly active and stable Ru‐based catalysts for the acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is essential to accelerate the industrialization of proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE). However, Ru‐based catalysts inevitably follow the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM) during the actual reaction, which in turn triggers severe Ru dissolution. While shifting the reaction pathway to the adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) improves stability, it often compromises catalytic activity. Herein, we design an Nb‐doped Ru/RuO2 heterostructure catalyst to inhibit the unstable LOM, and concurrently propose a favorable Brønsted Site‐Promoted Proton Transfer (BSPT) mechanism derived from the AEM. Specifically, the synergy between Nb doping and Ru/RuO2 heterostructure enhances activity by improving deprotonation capability and optimizing oxygen‐intermediate adsorption, while simultaneously improving durability by stabilizing lattice oxygen and suppressing excessive oxidation and dissolution of Ru. Consequently, the Nb‐Ru/RuO2 delivers an overpotential of 186 mV at 10 mA cm−2 with impressive durability over 3000 h. In a working PEMWE, it exhibits remarkable durability for 3000, 1200, and 900 h at 500, 1000, and 2000 mA cm−2. This study offers novel design principles and theoretical foundations to advance efficient, low‐cost PEMWE hydrogen production.

title: A Glycan Key Unlocks Microglia Targeting and Reprogramming to Promote Functional Recovery After Spinal Cord Injury
content:
A glycan ligand (2,5‐AM) functionalizes a pH‐responsive nanoparticle to target the microglia‐specific receptor GLUT5. Upon internalization into the acidic lysosome, the nanoparticle ICT@APD releases the agent icaritin (ICT), which reprograms microglia toward an anti‐inflammatory phenotype. Encapsulated within a hydrogel, this system enables sustained delivery, promoting axon regeneration, neuroprotection, and functional recovery in a mouse model of spinal cord injury (SCI).








ABSTRACT
Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers uncontrolled neuroinflammation driven by dysfunctional microglia and pro‐inflammatory‐biased reprogramming, yet precise therapeutic strategies remain limited. Here, we report a novel glycan‐targeted nanoparticle system (ICT@APD) designed to enhance the microglia‐reprogramming potential of icaritin (ICT) while overcoming its inherent narrow therapeutic window. By functionalizing nanoparticles with 2,5‐anhydro‐D‐mannitol (2,5‐AM), a high‐affinity ligand for the microglia‐specific transporter GLUT5, ICT@APD achieves selective microglial uptake and amplifies the capacity of ICT to reprogram microglia toward an anti‐inflammatory phenotype. The targeted reprogramming consequently creates a positive microenvironment that promotes axon regeneration, neuronal survival, and synaptic reconstruction, leading to significantly improved locomotor recovery after SCI. Our findings establish a novel glycan‐mediated microglial targeting and reprogramming strategy for SCI repair, which may extend to other central nervous system disorders and provide a referenceable platform for the delivery of other therapeutic agents with a narrow therapeutic window.

title: Emergent Molecular Weaving in an Ionic Metal‐Organic Network for CO2 Conversion
content:
A self‐templated 1D−1D ionic molecularly woven single‐crystal framework forms from Cu2+ and trinitrophloroglucinol (TNPG) in water. The woven lattice, stabilized by non‐covalent interactions and multiple Cu2+ geometries, exhibits dearomatized π‐cores and functions as a visible‐light photocatalyst for CO2 reduction upon mild thermal pre‐activation at 50°C.








ABSTRACT
Molecular weaving has emerged as a powerful design strategy in supramolecular chemistry, yet most woven frameworks rely on rigid ligands and elaborate templating. Here, we report a minimalistic, aqueous‐phase synthesis of a woven metal‐organic superstructure assembled from Cu2+ and 2,4,6‐trinitrobenzene‐1,3,5‐triol (TNPG). In the crystal, asymmetric coordination of TNPG with Cu2+ yields charged one‐dimensional (1D) polymeric strands featuring both distorted octahedral and square planar geometries. These strands interlace at a specific angle to form a two‐dimensional (2D) woven architecture, a rare 1D─1D topological weaving stabilized by hydrogen bonding. The structure also incorporates discrete Cu2+ cationic complexes, where metal coordination significantly perturbs the aromatic π‐conjugated system of TNPG. These cationic units are tethered within the network through strong hydrogen bonding and electrostatic attraction to the anionic woven strands, contributing to the structural integrity of the superstructure. Given the redox‐active Cu2+ centers, electronically modulated ligand environment, and framework stability, the Cu‐TNPG network was evaluated for visible‐light‐driven CO2 reduction. The photocatalytic performance of Cu‐TNPG originates from its high charge separation efficiency and abundant catalytically active sites. Moreover, mild thermal pre‐activation led to enhanced CO evolution efficiency through structural modulations, with a selectivity of ∼85% for CO over H2, highlighting its structural and functional versatility.

title: 3D Ordered Macroporous Cu‐Based Multimetallic Alloy Enables Efficient Asymmetric C–C Coupling for Selective CO2 Electroreduction to Ethylene
content:
Engineering a multimetallic alloy interface on a 3D ordered macroporous architecture effectively regulates the electronic distribution of Cuδ+ sites. This tailored microenvironment enhances local electric fields, accelerates interfacial mass transport, and promotes asymmetric *CO–*CHO coupling, delivering an outstanding ethylene Faradaic efficiency of 64.1% for electrochemical CO2 reduction under acidic conditions.








ABSTRACT
The abundant Cu0/Cuδ+ interfaces generated after reconstruction are crucial for promoting the coupling of *CO and *COH intermediates in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. However, Cu sites derived from a single metal severely restrict C–C coupling efficiency and product selectivity. Here, the direct regulation of the interfacial microenvironment is reported by constructing a 3D ordered macroporous (3DOM) architecture composed of multimetallic alloy (MMA) on the surface of CuOx. The designed catalyst exhibits superior Faradic efficiency of 64.1% for electrochemical CO2 reduction to ethylene at −1.55 V versus RHE under acidic conditions, and stability for over 60 h at 600 mA cm−2 in a flow cell. In‐situ experiments and theoretical simulations reveal that the 3DOM structure enhances the surface electric field, raises the local pH, and accelerates interfacial mass transport. The electronic structure of Cuδ+ (0<δ<1) sites at multimetallic interfaces is effectively regulated by other metals, inducing electronic heterogeneity and an asymmetric charge distribution on the Cu sites that facilitates asymmetric *CO–*CHO coupling. This work establishes the design principles for Cu‐based multimetallic alloy with atomic‐level customisation, demonstrating that the precise structural design and electronic structure of Cuδ+ sites could govern *CO adsorption and hydrogenation pathways, thereby enhancing ethylene selectivity.

title: Natural Versus Artificial Photosynthesis: Pushing Beyond Nature's Limits to Deliver Low‐Cost Solar Fuels
content:
Natural and artificial photosynthesis are compared through a function‐matched, level‐resolved, and boundary‐explicit framework spanning light harvesting, charge transfer, catalysis, photoprotection, repair, and system integration. The comparison reveals complementary strengths: artificial systems provide greater materials and reaction programmability, whereas natural photosynthesis retains distinctive capabilities in dynamic regulation, regeneration, repair, and multiscale coordination. These differences define design targets for durable and integrated solar‐to‐chemical systems.








ABSTRACT
Natural photosynthesis (NP) sustains life by coordinating light harvesting, charge separation, multielectron catalysis, carbon fixation, regulation, and repair. Artificial photosynthesis instead aims to convert solar energy selectively into fuels and chemicals through designed light absorbers, interfaces, and catalytic sites. This review compares the two systems across light harvesting, charge separation and transfer, catalytic conversion, photoprotection, and system integration, emphasizing that meaningful comparisons require similar functions, comparable metrics, and clearly defined system boundaries. Field‐scale NP typically operates at sub‐percent solar‐to‐biomass efficiencies, whereas selected artificial photosynthetic devices have achieved double‐digit solar‐to‐fuel efficiencies under defined conditions. These values should not be directly ranked because the products and system functions differ. We identify the respective strengths of artificial systems in spectral, interfacial, catalytic, and product control, and of natural systems in regulation, repair, regeneration, and multiscale coordination, providing design principles for efficient, durable, and scalable solar‐to‐chemical conversion.

title: Anti‐Poisoning Tin Single‐Atom Unlocks High‐Activity Ruthenium Catalysts for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
content:
We report an anti‐poisoning strategy for alkaline hydrogen evolution by engineering single‐atom Sn into RuO2@Ru catalysts, wherein atomically dispersed Sn modulates adjacent Ru sites via Sn─O─Ru bonds to simultaneously weaken *OH binding and optimize *H adsorption. The resulting Sn1‐RuO2@Ru/C achieves an ultralow overpotential of 9 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and maintains stable operation for over 300 h in an anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer (AEMWE).








ABSTRACT
The practical deployment of anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer (AEMWE) is constrained by the lack of efficient electrocatalysts for the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), primarily due tothe sluggishVolmer step and inefficient intermediate desorption. While Ru‐based catalysts exhibit promising *H binding energy, their practical performance is compromised by poor water dissociation kinetics and susceptibility to active‐site blockage by adsorbed species. Herein, we report a Sn‐doped RuO2@Ru catalyst supported on carbon black, wherein atomically dispersed Sn modulates the electronic structure of RuO2 via Sn─O bonds, simultaneously facilitating water dissociation, optimizing *H adsorption, and preventing *OH poisoning. The catalyst achieves exceptional performance with an overpotential of 9 mV at 10 mA cm−2, positioning it among the most active HER catalysts reported to date. When integrated into a full AEMWE, it operates at 1.85 V and 1000 mA cm−2 with stability exceeding 300 h. Mechanistic studies suggest that Sn doping fine‐tunes the *OH and *H binding energies, addressing the kinetic imbalance inherent in conventional Ru catalysts. This work highlights the effectiveness of atomic‐level electronic engineering via an anti‐poisoning strategy for designing efficient, stable alkaline HER electrocatalysts toward industrial hydrogen production.

title: Engineering Thermoelectric‐Electrocatalytic Coupling in RuO2/PrCoO3 Heterointerface for Efficient Oxygen Evolution
content:
This work establishes thermoelectric‐electrocatalytic coupling by constructing an Ohmic RuO2/PrCoO3 heterointerface for efficient oxygen evolution. The thermoelectric potential generated under a mild temperature gradient selectively activates the intrinsically inert RuO2 (101) facet, reducing overpotential at 10 mA cm−2 to 178 mV and enabling stable operation of anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer at 2.0 A cm−2 for 600 hours.








ABSTRACT
The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is pivotal for diverse electrochemical energy conversion systems; however, it has so far been plagued by sluggish kinetics and excessive energy consumption. In this study, we proposed an innovative thermoelectric‐electrocatalytic coupling strategy to enhance OER efficiency by constructing an Ohmic heterointerface through uniform integration of RuO2 with thermoelectric oxide (PrCoO3). Combined experimental and theoretical analyses revealed that the thermoelectric potential generated by PrCoO3 selectively activates the intrinsically inert (101) facet of RuO2 by lowering *OOH formation barrier, thereby substantially boosting the overall OER performance. Consequently, the RuO2/PrCoO3 heterointerface delivered exceptional OER performance under a mild temperature gradient (ΔT) of 175°C, achieving dramatic reduction in overpotential at 10 mA cm−2 from 300 mV (ΔT = 0°C) to 178 mV, 4 300% increase in current density, and negligible potential loss over 1,000 h. When the catalyst was assembled into an anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer, the cell driven by spontaneous heating reached a low voltage of 2.18 V at a current density of 2.0 A cm−2, with stable operation for 600 h. These insights into harnessing thermal gradient via integrated electrocatalytic system are crucial for the recovery of industrial waste heat and its conversion into high‐value chemicals.
